item.title: Atmoce targets commercial and industrial sector with its flexible AC stackable storage
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Atmoce has introduced its AC stackable extra-low voltage storage solution in Australia and follows the September start of the peak demand reduction battery incentive scheme for businesses in NSW.
item.content:encoded:
Germany-headquartered energy technology company Atmoce is launching its AC stackable extra-low voltage storage solution in Australia and follows the September 2026 start of the Peak Demand Reduction Scheme (PDRS) for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses in New South Wales (NSW).

Introducing the M-ELV BattBank in Australia at All Energy Australia 2026, the new solution comprises a modular AC architecture operating below 60 V DC, with each BattBank cluster accommodating up to seven battery packs, delivering up to 112 kWh.

Capacity can be expanded in 16 kWh increments to suit individual site requirements.

Independent module operation helps support system continuity if a battery module fails, while 0.25C–0.5C adjustable power enables peak shaving and energy shifting.

Atmoce said the solution’s modular, scalable architecture is well suited to the expanded NSW PDRS, including battery energy storage system (BESS)5 installations above 200 kWh and up to 30 MWh.

Since 1 September 2026, eligible C&I installations in NSW can receive approximately 20–40% discounts through the PDRS scheme, depending on the installation.

15-year M-ELV Battery Warranty for Australia

Atmoce has also extended the warranty for its residential M-ELV Battery (MS-7K-U) to 15 years, which provides coverage for 15 years or 29.2 MWh of energy throughput, with a minimum 60% state of health retained, whichever comes first.

The M-ELV battery uses an extra-low voltage AC architecture operating below 30 Vdc, designed to reduce risks associated with high-voltage DC while supporting flexible residential energy system integration.

The warranty is Australia-wide and extends to eligible MS-7K-U units already shipped or being installed.

item.title: SMA grid-forming DC-hybrid solution unveiled at All Energy Australia
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: SMA Australia has unveiled a new grid-forming solar and battery solution at All Energy Australia, which tackles the key developer challenges of securing grid connections and attracting investment.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-based SMA Australia, a subsidiary of German solar and battery inverter manufacturer SMA Solar Technology AG, has unveiled a new grid-forming solution at All Energy in Melbourne, which tackles the challenges of securing grid connections and attracting investment.

The solution enables renewable generation to actively support electricity system stability through services including synthetic inertia, fast frequency response and voltage support.

Its DC-coupled architecture can capture solar energy otherwise lost through inverter clipping and storing it for dispatch during periods of higher electricity demand or more favourable market conditions.

It combines power conversion technology, intelligent plant controls and engineering support, helping reduce system integration complexity and the challenge of coordinating equipment and control systems from multiple suppliers.

It also incorporates advanced silicon carbide semiconductor technology, enabling DC-side conversion efficiencies of up to 99.%.

SMA Australia Managing Director John Alexander, who will address All Energy on Wednesday 28 October in a presentation titled ‘From megawatts to megabankable: How grid stability is reshaping renewable energy finance’, said the next phase of Australia’s energy transition won’t be measured by how many projects are announced but by how many actually connect to the grid, perform reliably and deliver a return.

“Grid stability is no longer just an engineering issue. It goes directly to investment confidence and long-term project value,” Alexander said.

“Developers and investors need confidence that their assets can perform reliably today and adapt to the needs of tomorrow’s electricity system. That means designing for Australia’s unique grid conditions, managing risk from the outset and preparing for evolving grid requirements and future market opportunities.”

Alexander said Australia has some of the most demanding grid connection requirements in the world and developers need more than technology that performs well in isolation.

“They need integrated solutions designed for Australian conditions, backed by local engineering expertise and long-term support,” Alexander said.

Medium voltage power station

Also on display at All Energy, SMA will showcase its 40-foot Medium Voltage Power Station (MVPS) 6400–10000 range.

Its integrated architecture, featuring redundant inverter technology, is designed to improve plant availability and support reliable operation of large-scale renewable energy projects.

Other power infrastructure solutions for artificial intelligence (AI) and hyperscale data centres displayed at the SMA Australia exhibit include GridAssist, GridLink AC and the planned GridLink DC architecture.

item.title: Trinasolar targets rooftops with ‘Australian-exclusive’ full-black module
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Trinasolar has announced an Australian-exclusive all-black version of its Vertex S+ G3 dual-glass TOPCon modules for residential and commercial applications. The new products deliver up to 510 W of power output with 24.4% efficiency.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese PV module manufacturer Trinasolar will unveil a full-black dual-glass TOPCon solar module for residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) applications at the All Energy Australia conference starting in Melbourne on Wednesday.

Edison Zhou, Trina’s head of operations in Australia, New Zealand and Pacific Islands, said the “Australian-exclusive” Vertex S+ G3 Full Black solar module marks the return of the company’s all-black offering, combining its distinctive design with next-generation TOPCon 3.0 technology.

“Black is back with more power, greater efficiency and next-generation solar technology,” he said. “The Vertex S+ G3 combines the premium all-black design customers want with the performance and reliability they expect from Trinasolar.”

The Vertex S+ G3 is built on Trinasolar’s n-type i-TOPCon Ultra technology, and features “zero-gap” stacked welding and “zero-string bar” technologies.

Trinasolar is offering five variants, with power output ranging from 490 W to 510 W and power conversion efficiencies between 23.5% and 24.4%. Open-circuit voltage ranges from 39.4 V to 40.0 V, while short-circuit current is between 15.91 A and 15.97 A.

The panels feature 1.6 mm glass front and back in a black anodised aluminium frame. They measure 1,842 mm x 1,134 mm x 30 mm and weigh 21.95 kg.

They can be deployed in systems with a maximum voltage of 1,500 V and feature IP68-rated junction boxes. The temperature coefficient is -0.26% per C, with an operating temperature range of -40 C to 70 C.

The modules are backed by a 25-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty. First-year degradation is specified at less than 1.0%, with 30-year end-of-life output guaranteed at no less than 88.5% of nominal power.

Trinasolar said the new panels are compatible with mainstream inverters and diverse mounting systems and have been manufactured in response to “strong demand from Australian homeowners, businesses and installers for high-performance solar that doesn’t compromise on appearance.”

The Vertex S+ G3 is part of a broader product portfolio that Trinasolar will unveil at All Energy.

The company will also use the event to launch its C&I Integrated Engineering & Solutions product, that will combine project-specific engineering, system optimisation and selective components sourcing, including solar modules, mounting and tracking systems, and battery energy storage solutions (BESS).

Trinasolar said the expansion of the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) on 1 October 2026 to qualifying solar installations above 100 kW and up to 1 MW creates new opportunities for C&I solar.

“As C&I projects increasingly integrate solar, battery storage and energy management technologies, Trina Solutions provides tailored support through close consultation with a dedicated team, leveraging global engineering experience to address immediate priorities and anticipate future needs,” the company said, adding  that “businesses and developers can benefit from integrated energy solutions, while EPCs and system integrators can leverage Trinasolar’s technologies and expertise to complement their existing capabilities for end-to-end project execution.”

Trinasolar also said it would use the All Energy event to showcase its wider solar and energy storage portfolio, including the 6.25 MWh Elementa 3 battery, which brings together DC technology with AC-side integration capabilities.

item.title: Western Australia targets 75% renewables share for main grid
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Western Australia has committed to a renewable energy target of 75% by 2030-2031 for its main electricity grid as it prepares for the retirement of state-owned coal-fired power stations by the end of this decade.
item.content:encoded:
The Western Australia (WA) government aims to achieve 75% renewable electricity on the South West Interconnected System (SWIS) by 2030-2031, supported by large-scale solar, wind, and battery energy storage projects.

The target doubles the previous goal of 40% and comes as the state prepares to exit coal-fired power by 2030.

The state government said the renewable energy target (RET) is complemented by a Made in WA Energy Affordability Investment Program that will provide low-interest loans of up to $15 million (USD 10.5 million) to help manufacturers install solar and battery systems and upgrade equipment to take advantage of cheaper energy. 

WA Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the new 75% target is a “statement of intent” that is designed to encourage private sector investment.

“We know that renewables, backed by storage and gas, is the cheapest and most reliable energy mix for Western Australia,” she said. “That’s why we’re powering ahead with our support for the energy opportunities of the future and encouraging businesses to invest in WA.”

The government’s commitment has been welcomed by climate advocacy collaborative Solutions for Climate WA and its alliance of business, industry, investors, unions, and advocacy bodies.

Solutions for Climate WA Director Jessica Panegyres said the new target is a key step forward for the state’s energy future.

“[This] makes it clear that the future of our electricity system is renewables,” she said. “A renewable energy target sends an important signal to the businesses, investors, workers and communities who will deliver WA’s next generation of energy infrastructure.”

WA has some of the best renewable energy resources in the world and a strong industrial base and Panegyres said setting a target provides the certainty required to turn that potential into investment on the ground.

Panegyres said the next task is making sure WA has a credible pathway to achieve its goal.

“That means continuing to accelerate investment in renewable energy generation, storage and the transmission infrastructure needed to connect it, while ensuring communities and regional areas share in the benefits,” she said.

Smart Energy Council (SEC) State Manager John Welch said WA’s new renewable energy target will advance the rate of growth for the state’s renewable energy industry

“Our members across solar, wind and battery storage are ready to build in WA, and a target gives them a clear goal to build towards,” he said, adding that transmission will be critical to achieving the target.

“The priority now is to keep the grid build moving and lock in dates for its next stages,” he said.

item.title: World’s largest battery-electric ship begins commercial service
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: The world’s largest electric ship, constructed by Australia shipbuilder Incat Tasmania, has officially entered commercial service in South America.
item.content:encoded:
The 130-metre China Zorrilla, built by Incat Tasmania for South American ferry operator Buquebus, has completed its maiden commercial voyage across the River Plate (Rio de la Plata), between Buenos Aires and Uruguay.

Incat said the battery-electric catamaran, the largest electric vehicle of any type on the planet, has officially entered commercial service, carrying passengers on the 55-kilometre journey between Buenos Aires and Colonia.

The vessel, known during construction as Hull 096, is fitted with more than 5,000 Corvus Energy Dolphin NxtGen battery modules weighing more than 250 tonnes, about four times larger than any battery previously installed in a ship.

The energy storage system delivers more than 40 MWh installed capacity, powering eight electrically driven waterjets.

The vessel, that can carry up to 2,100 passengers and 225 vehicles, has a 90-minute range, and cruises at about 25 knots (approximately 46 km/h).

The ship is supported by dedicated high-power charging infrastructure at terminals on both sides of the river, allowing its batteries to be recharged between crossings with a 60-90 minute charge time.

Incat Chairmain Robert Clifford described the ferry’s first passenger service as a historic moment for the future of sustainable shipping.

“This ship proves that large, high-capacity commercial vessels can operate on electric power,” he said.

For Incat, the milestone is also part of a broader shift toward electric vessel construction. The shipbuilder is currently building three 129 m battery-electric ferries for Danish operator Molslinjen, along with two 78 m hybrid-electric vessels at its Hobart facility.

item.title: Fuel shocks make investment in renewables an energy security priority
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australia’s energy transition is now as much about energy security as the push for net zero. With global fuel markets increasingly volatile, the pace of Australia’s renewable energy transition will help determine how exposed businesses remain to international energy shocks, and how competitive our industries can be.
item.content:encoded:
Recent global fuel shocks have exposed Australia’s vulnerability to international oil markets. From February to the end of March, oil prices surged from about US$71 to nearly US$127 a barrel, while Australian wholesale diesel prices climbed from $1.65 to more than $3.10 per litre. With Westpac warning that prolonged conflict could push oil prices towards US$150 a barrel in 2027, energy security is now as compelling a reason to accelerate the transition to renewables as the push for net zero.

Australia is the world’s largest diesel importer, sourcing about 87% of its diesel from overseas. Our transport-heavy economy is also unusually diesel-intensive, consuming about three times as much diesel per dollar of GDP as the US and Japan. Electrifying more of the vehicles and equipment that consume it would reduce our vulnerability to global supply shocks. For the renewables and storage industry, the opportunity extends beyond replacing coal-fired electricity: it lies in helping businesses replace imported fuels with locally generated power.

Superpower Institute modelling suggests electrification and domestic low-carbon fuels could lift Australia’s fuel security from 17% to 87% by 2040. These are modelled scenarios, and low-carbon fuels account for part of the improvement. But the scale warrants attention from investors and policymakers.

As imported fossil fuels become more expensive and difficult to get, freight operators, miners and other businesses switching from diesel will become new electricity customers. The pace of their conversion will depend on whether they can secure reliable supply and justify the capital expenditure.

Australia is a world leader in rooftop solar. Grid-scale storage and household batteries are helping shift renewable electricity into the evening. The next gains will come from electrifying diesel-reliant sectors that previously considered the switch too costly.

Each time global fuel supplies are disrupted, the business case for this investment becomes stronger.

Electric buses are more expensive than diesel-powered buses to purchase. The Commonwealth Bank nevertheless estimates lifetime savings of about $275,000 per bus. Operators must be willing to commit more capital upfront in order to see the long-run savings, but fuel-price volatility strengthens the case for making the investment now to manage higher prices later.

Likewise, Energy Futures Foundation modelling suggests a coordinated five-year program could support 30,000 to 50,000 electric trucks, displacing up to one billion litres of diesel annually.

These examples demonstrate the scale of the potential savings for operators. Repeated across fleets and sectors, businesses’ individual investment decisions will reduce Australia’s exposure to international oil markets while driving demand for domestic electricity.

Yet, to make the switch, businesses need confidence that renewable electricity supply will keep up. Investing in new equipment locks in electricity costs for years. Reliable, competitively priced power over the life of the asset is vital to ensure the case stacks up.

To give businesses the confidence to switch, Australia needs to increase investment in renewable generation and storage to replace retiring coal plants and meet growing electricity demand. In NSW alone, AEMO forecasts operational demand rising from around 64 TWh in 2026 to 85 TWh by 2035.

And while data centres have attracted considerable attention as a major source of future electricity demand, road transport electrification represents an opportunity of comparable scale. Nationally, AEMO’s 2026 Integrated System Plan projects annual electricity consumption from corporate fleets and commercial vehicles will reach around 31 TWh by 2050, compared with approximately 34 TWh from data centres. Importantly, electric vehicle charging offers greater flexibility than the concentrated, relatively constant demand of data centres.

As electric freight fleets expand, charging demand will be spread across depots, logistics hubs and major transport corridors. With smart charging, this demand could be better aligned with renewable generation, including solar, improving network utilisation and potentially reducing system costs. For distribution network service providers, this presents an opportunity to accommodate growing electricity demand while unlocking greater value from existing infrastructure.

Increased storage capacity will be critical. AEMO-based analysis indicates NSW could need about 53 GWh of utility-scale storage by 2030, dwarfing the 12.5 GWh currently operating or under construction. Much of the required capacity is yet to secure finance, highlighting the scale of the investment opportunity for the renewables and storage industry.

Each business that switches from imported diesel to domestically generated electricity reduces its exposure to global fuel markets. Across freight, mining and industry, these individual decisions could collectively transform Australia’s energy security.

The next phase of Australia’s energy transition is not just about how we generate electricity, but how we use it. For the renewables and storage industry, the opportunity extends well beyond replacing coal-fired power. It lies in powering a more productive, resilient and energy-secure Australian economy.

Author: Katerina Kimmorley, Commissioner with the NSW Net Zero Commission and a Board Member of the NSW Energy Security Corporation

item.title: Sigenergy unveils 401 kWh all-in-one battery for C&I sites
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Sigenergy has introduced a new 401 kWh all-in-one battery unit that can be scaled to more than 4 MWh into Australia as it prepares for a “wave of growth” in the C&I energy storage sector.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese manufacturer Sigenergy has unveiled a 401 kWh battery energy storage system for commercial and industrial (C&I) installations.

The company said the SigenCube fully integrates the power conversion, energy management, and batteries in a single cabinet. The modular architecture has been engineered for high scalability and supports up to 100 units in parallel.

Sigenergy, which has established itself as one of Australia’s most popular residential battery suppliers with more than 120,000 systems already installed here, said the product has been designed to satisfy expected growth in the C&I energy storage sector following the federal government’s recent expansion of the small-scale renewable energy scheme (SRES).

The expansion, that took effect on 1 October, lifted the maximum size of solar systems covered under existing Small-scale Technology Certificate mechanism from 100 kW to 1 MW capacity, increasing demand for both solar panels and storage as C&I companies look to generate and store more of their own power.

Will Hall, Managing Director of Sigenergy in Australia and New Zealand, said the changes dictate that the next wave of growth in storage will be commercial.

“Home batteries have gone mainstream in Australia, and businesses now want the same control over their power costs and reliability,” he said. “SigenCube is our answer for the sites where space, noise and heavy loads have held storage back.”

Sigenstore said the SigneCube is built to meet heavy industrial demands. Each ES401 cabinet holds 401 kWh in a 1,100 mm × 2,450 mm × 1,650 mm footprint, delivering an energy density of more than 220 kWh per square metre. The manufacturer said for a 4 MWh project, SigenCube needs 54.5 m², compared with more than 80 m² for traditional solutions, a saving of more than 30%.

“Businesses are not only asking for more kWh. They want a system that fits on a tight site, runs quietly next to its neighbours and keeps the plant going when the grid does not,” Hall said. “That is what SigenCube is built to do.”

Every cabinet has its own energy management system, and up to 100 units can run in parallel without an external data logger. Operating temperatures range from -30°C to 55°C. Units feature AI-assisted thermal management, active battery balancing, and declared sound level below 60 dB.

Protection runs from the battery pack to the whole system, including a top explosion vent, smoke and heat detection, cabinet-level aerosol suppression, a water firefighting interface and multiple layers of overcurrent protection. Asealed cooling loop gives a 10-year coolant life.

Sigenergy said grid-forming capability delivers 0 ms load-side disruption and MWh-level black start without grid support, with SigenCube capable of 150% overload for 10 seconds.

Units are pre-commissioned at the factory, and basic setup and diagnostics take up to five minutes on site through the app.

SigenCube will be available in Australia for off-grid projects and in New Zealand from January 2027. Grid-connected projects in Australia will follow Clean Energy Council listing.

item.title: Proa launches new platform to optimise renewable energy asset operations
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian energy technology company Proa Energy has unveiled an integrated software platform designed to simplify and optimise how large-scale solar, wind, battery and hybrid assets are operated.
item.content:encoded:
Proa Energy said its Nexo platform brings the company’s renewable energy solutions together in one operating system that connects plant data, forecasting, bidding, dispatch management, performance analytics, reporting and operational workflows.

The Melbourne-based company said the Nexo platform combines its software and on-site hardware solutions to give asset managers, traders, operational teams and external providers a clearer and more consistent view of performance across assets and portfolios while its modular architecture enables them to select the capabilities relevant to their assets and add new modules as their operational requirements and portfolios evolve.

“Nexo is not an additional layer sitting alongside our existing technology. It is the platform that brings our solutions together,” Proa founder and Chief Executive Officer Victor Depoorter said.

“Nexo represents a major step change. It connects plant data, market intelligence and team workflows within one operating environment. It aims at maximising the effectiveness and predictability of renewable assets, which translates into maximised revenue for stakeholders and owners.”

“Our vision is to power the global transition to clean energy by improving performance, cost and reliability across every asset.”

Proa said 12 renewable energy projects across Australia have already adopted or are onboarding Nexo, representing more than 2 GW of contracted capacity. These include two hybrid projects, with the remaining projects spanning stand-alone large-scale solar, wind and battery assets.

Among the projects are four of Vena Energy’s assets in Queensland and South Australia and Potentia Energy’s Quorn Park hybrid project near Parkes in western New South Wales.

The Quorn Park facility, the first large scale solar-battery hybrid power plant to be built on the National Electricity Market, combines an 80 MW solar farm and a 20 MW / 40 MWh battery behind the same connection point.

Potentia Energy Chief Operations Officer Gabriele Mallarini said the Nexo platform is a key part of maximising the performance of the Quorn Park project.

“Nexo is now part of how we operate the project every day, and we’re excited by its potential to help us unlock the full value of hybrid assets,” he said.

Proa, which recently secured $4.1 million in funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency to develop a platform to help solar farm operators detect faults, improve performance, and cut operating costs, said the launch of Nexo marks the company’s evolution from a forecasting and monitoring specialist into an integrated renewable energy intelligence partner.

“Nexo is our latest milestone and the foundation for what comes next. It gives us a platform to integrate new hardware, develop new tools and keep improving how renewable energy assets operate,” Depoorter said.

“The energy transition requires more than building new infrastructure. We also need to get more from every asset: better performance, more predictable operations and greater value from the investment already made.”

item.title: Australian renewable energy investment surges to new heights
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Five renewable energy projects totalling 1.4 GW of new generation capacity and 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of battery energy storage capacity came online across Australia in the first six months of 2026 while 12 generation projects totalling 2.6 GW of new capacity reached a final investment decision during the same period.
item.content:encoded:
A new report shows that more renewable generation capacity – led predominantly by solar farms and hybrid solar-and-battery projects – reached financial close, and more large-scale battery energy storage was switched on across Australia in the first half of the year than across all of 2025.

The Clean Energy Council’s (CEC) Bi-annual investment report: Large-scale renewable generation and storage (January-June 2026) also shows that five generation projects totalling 1.4 GW of new capacity and worth more than $2.8 billion (USD 1.97 billion) were commissioned and started operations during the first half of this year.

The CEC said the rolling 12-month quarterly average for newly commissioned capacity has now reached 912 MW, up 56% compared to the same period 12 months ago, and the highest rolling average seen since Q1 2022. A further eight generation projects totalling about 1.9 GW began construction in H1 2026.

In addition to the new generation projects, nine battery energy storage projects worth $4.3 billion and representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity were also switched on in the first six months of the year, surpassing the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh added during 2025.

The report also shows that more new generation capacity reached financial close across Australia in the first half of 2026 than in the whole of 2025 with 12 projects totalling 2.6 GW securing finance, compared with 2.3 GW across all of last year. Utility-scale solar drove the new commitments with 11 of the 12 projects solar or solar hybrids with one onshore wind project also reaching financial close.

A further 13 large-scale battery energy storage projects totalling 1.6 GW / 6.5 GWh also reached financial close in H1 2026, including a record 6.3 GWh in the June quarter.

CEC Chief Executive Officer Jackie Trad said the results show the resilience and growth of the clean energy industry in the face of difficult headwinds.

“Australian sun and wind cannot be cut off by conflict overseas,” she said. “Each new solar, wind and battery investment helps make Australia more energy independent and economically resilient, shielding Australians from global fossil fuel price shocks and supply disruptions.”

The CEC said there are now 141 renewable energy generation and battery energy storage projects worth around $32.5 billion are now funded or under construction across Australia. This includes 76 generation projects totalling 11.7 GW and 79 storage projects, either standalone or hybrid projects, equivalent to 12.6 GW / 35 GWh.  

Solar accounts for 53% of generation capacity at financial close or under construction, and Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and Western Australia all share approximately 27% of solar capacity either at financial close or under construction,

Queensland holds the largest share of pipeline investment, accounting for $9.6 billion and 4.5 GW in projects that are currently at financial close or are under construction. NSW has the largest battery storage pipeline at 4.3 GW / 11.2 GWh.

“Queensland is leading the nation in clean energy investment, showing what can be achieved when world-class renewable energy resources are matched with investor confidence,” Trad said.

“But the story is bigger than any one state or territory; across Australia, investors are backing the technologies they know will power our economic future and strengthen our energy security.”

Trad did however warn that clean energy investment is not immune to tougher conditions and said confidence appears to be softening, particularly for onshore wind, with investors naming approvals and transmission as their biggest obstacles.

“With $32.5 billion worth of generation and storage projects now under construction or at financial close, maintaining this momentum will require predictable approvals, timely transmission and long-term revenue certainty to help more projects, including onshore wind, progress into operation,” she said.

item.title: Array teams with Australia’s Aeeris to address hail risk for large-scale solar
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: United States-based solar tracker manufacturer Array Technologies has teamed with environmental services company Aeeris to help address hail risk for owners and operators of utility-scale solar assets in Australia.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-headquartered Aeeris, through its wholly-owned subsidiary Early Warning Network (EWN), announced it has partnered with Array Technologies to expand the automated hail response capabilities of the manufacturer’s SmarTrack software platform in Australia.

EWN’s real-time hail detection and forecasting systems – that combine Australia-wide radar coverage, meteorologist verification, and proprietary detection algorithms to identify hail risks for solar projects – have been integrated into Array’s SmarTrack hail alert response platform.

Array said its SmarTrack software analyses the EWN intelligence and, coupled with automated tracker response, adjusts solar modules to maximum tilt protective angles ahead of severe weather, without the need for human decision-making.

Aeeris Executive Chairman Henrik Thorup said the solution provides Australian solar farm operators with an automated, weather-response defence designed to mitigate one of the sector’s escalating operational risks.

“As solar projects continue to be deployed across Australia, this advancement will better help to protect these valuable energy assets on the grid from the rising risks of damaging hail,” he said. “We look forward to working with Array to ensure that solar power continues to play a valuable role for the Australian power grid through the built-in resilience needed to be protected from hail threats.”

Australia’s large-scale solar sector has scaled from less 350 MW of deployed capacity in 2017 to more than 13 GW by the end of 2025, and much of that build-out sits in regions prone to severe convective storms.

Green transition underwriting business Tokio Marine GX (TMGX) recently identified hail as an escalating risk across that growing footprint.

Francesca Lucia Falcone, Array’s business development director in the Asia Pacific, said as solar expands into hail-prone regions, EWN’s capabilities help Array provide solar farm operators with a clear way of showing insurers and financiers how they actively manage risk and support long-term asset longevity as the sector grows.

“This integration greatly improves the bankability of these projects,” she said, adding that the collaboration complements Array’s existing architecture.

Array said its trackers utilise an AC grid-powered motor and wired communications rather than relying on battery power and wireless communications, that can be disrupted by extreme weather.

“Array’s approach to engineered simplicity combined with EWN’s hail intelligence platform unlocks new potential for Australia that will continuously benefit solar projects by equipping them with tools that make them adaptable when facing hail risks,” Falcone said.
